prompt.text: Which genus and phylum are shown?
prompt.imageAlt: Blue-stained microscope view of branching filaments. Some filaments end in a brush of narrow cells tipped with chains of round spores.
prompt.caption: Source photomicrograph at 570×. CDC / Dr. Lucille K. Georg, Public Health Image Library ID 26587.

questions.explanation: This is *Penicillium*, in Ascomycota. The conidiophores end in brush-like clusters of conidia, called penicilli, and the hyphae have cross-walls. Ascomycetes make asexual spores called conidia at the tips of hyphae. *Aspergillus* is also in Ascomycota and also makes chains of conidia, but they radiate from a swollen vesicle rather than a branched brush. *Saccharomyces* is an ascomycete yeast of single budding cells, without these hyphae and conidiophores. *Rhizopus* is in Zygomycota and carries its spores inside a round sporangium. The photograph is a cropped detail from CDC / Dr. Lucille K. Georg, Public Health Image Library ID 26587.

questions.explanation: This is *Aspergillus*, in Ascomycota. The conidiophore ends in a swollen vesicle, and chains of conidia radiate from cells covering that vesicle. *Penicillium* is also in Ascomycota, but its conidia form a branched brush rather than radiating from a round vesicle. *Saccharomyces* is an ascomycete yeast of single budding cells, without this stalk and vesicle. *Rhizopus* is in Zygomycota and carries its spores inside a round sporangium. prompt.text: Which genus and phylum are shown?
prompt.imageAlt: Longitudinal section of a cone. Scale-like leaves surround chambers. Some chambers hold many tiny red spores, and others hold a few much larger spores.
prompt.caption: Longitudinal section of a strobilus. University of Wisconsin-Madison Department of Botany.

questions.explanation: This is *Selaginella*, a spike moss in Lycophyta. The section is a strobilus, a cone of spore-bearing leaves. Some sporangia are packed with many small microspores, and others hold a few large megaspores. That difference in spore size is heterospory. *Lycopodium* is also in Lycophyta and also makes a strobilus, but its spores are all one size. *Equisetum* makes a strobilus too, but it is a horsetail in Monilophyta and its spores are one size. A moss in Bryophyta releases spores from a capsule on a stalk, not from a strobilus of sporophylls. The section is from the University of Wisconsin-Madison Department of Botany.

questions.explanation: This is *Peziza*, a cup fungus in Ascomycota. The hymenium is a palisade of asci. Its hymenium is made of basidia, and the spores sit on the outside of those cells rather than inside a sac. *Rhizopus* is in Zygomycota and carries its spores inside a round sporangium.

There are no hyphae, conidiophores, or sporangia. *Penicillium* and *Aspergillus* are also in Ascomycota, but they grow as hyphae and release chains of conidia. *Rhizopus* is in Zygomycota and carries its spores inside a round sporangium. questions.explanation: This is *Rhizopus*, in Zygomycota. The dark, thick-walled bodies are zygosporangia, formed where two hyphae meet during sexual reproduction. The swollen cells against them are suspensors. The hyphae lack cross-walls. *Penicillium* and *Aspergillus* are in Ascomycota and release chains of conidia from hyphae that have cross-walls. *Saccharomyces* is an ascomycete yeast of single budding cells. prompt.text: Which phylum is shown?

questions.explanation: This is a moss, so the phylum is Bryophyta. The section is a male head. The long sacs are antheridia, and sperm form inside them. The sterile filaments among the antheridia are paraphyses. A paraphysis cut across looks like a small circle, and many end in a swollen tip. Hepatophyta are the liverworts. Their sex organs are borne on a stalked receptacle, rather than in a leafy tip like this. Lycophyta, such as *Selaginella*, make spores in a strobilus. Monilophyta include the horsetails, such as *Equisetum*, and those spores also form in a strobilus. The photograph is by Kristi Yim and is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons.

prompt.text: Which phylum does this gametophyte belong to?

questions.explanation: This gametophyte belongs to Monilophyta. The flat body has a notch, and hairlike rhizoids grow from the lower side. On the larger one, a small leaf and a root arise from the notch. Those belong to the young sporophyte, which is still attached to the gametophyte. A moss gametophyte in Bryophyta is a leafy shoot and releases spores from a capsule on a stalk. A liverwort gametophyte in Hepatophyta has a flat body and bears its sex organs on a stalked receptacle. A club moss in Lycophyta has a stem covered with many small leaves, and its gametophyte is not a free-living flat body like this. The photograph is by Curtis Clark and is licensed CC BY-SA 3.0 on Wikimedia Commons.

prompt.text: Complete the sentence identifying the function of a sorus, an annulus, and an indusium.

blanks: a cluster of sporangia on the underside of a leaf
the ring of cells that splits a sporangium open and flings out the spores
a flap of tissue that covers a young sorus
bank: a cluster of sporangia on the underside of a leaf
the ring of cells that splits a sporangium open and flings out the spores
a flap of tissue that covers a young sorus
the flat body that produces eggs and sperm
a jointed stem with leaves in whorls
questions.explanation: A sorus is a cluster of sporangia, usually on the underside of a fern leaf. An annulus is a ring of thick-walled cells on a sporangium. As those cells dry, the sporangium splits open and the annulus flings the spores outward. An indusium is a flap of tissue that covers a young sorus and protects the developing sporangia. The flat body that produces eggs and sperm is the gametophyte. A jointed stem with leaves in whorls is a horsetail, such as *Equisetum*.

prompt.text: Is *Selaginella* homosporous or heterosporous?

questions.explanation: *Selaginella* is heterosporous. Some sporangia hold many small microspores, and others hold a few large megaspores. *Lycopodium* is homosporous. Its spores are all one size.

prompt.text: Is *Lycopodium* homosporous or heterosporous?

questions.explanation: *Lycopodium* is homosporous. Its spores are all one size. *Selaginella* is heterosporous. Some of its sporangia hold many small microspores, and others hold a few large megaspores.
